title: Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026)
author: Ruth Appel · Maxim Massenkoff · Peter McCrory · Miles McCain · Ryan Heller · Tyler Neylon · Alex Tamkin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: Anthropic accepts the distinction between raw task speedups and aggregate productivity, then materially develops it by quantifying how reliability adjustments and complementary-task bottlenecks reduce projected gains. Its results are model-based projections rather than realised economy-wide outcomes, and it leaves employment effects contingent rather than settled.
qs: This is consistent with the fact that there is a larger share of API traffic concentrated in fewer tasks and associated occupations as compared to [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.f59e8ddf-c0a1-4146-baf7-80498800ed56): When tasks are complements, this concentration amplifies the bottleneck problem; when they are substitutes, it amplifies productivity gains from task specialization.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core distinction between observed AI use and actual displacement, then materially develops it with task-weighted exposure, occupation-specific deskilling and expertise scenarios, and quantified reliability-adjusted productivity projections. It does not directly establish reduced junior hiring, but provides mechanisms and measurement cautions consistent with stable aggregate employment masking uneven restructuring.
qs: However, its implications depend on how often these Claude conversations actually displace or augment work that would otherwise be done by humans.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s task-reconfiguration and supervised-augmentation account, while materially extending it with real-world usage measures that incorporate task importance, success rates and user behaviour. Its evidence that impacts depend on reliability, bottleneck tasks and skill composition reinforces the cluster’s caution against inferring general autonomy, productivity or displacement from technical capability alone, though it is economy-wide rather than legal-specific.
qs: As our effective AI coverage framework illustrates, the labor market implications for different workers will hinge on how reliable frontier AI tools are for their most central tasks.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between observed task use, successful performance and actual labour displacement. It materially develops that proposition by weighting coverage by task success, time and frequency, and by showing that reliability and task complementarity substantially reduce modelled productivity gains. Its results remain conditional estimates rather than evidence of realised job loss or growth.
qs: However, its implications depend on how often these Claude conversations actually displace or augment work that would otherwise be done by humans.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s task-level, jagged-capability framing and materially extends it with measures that weight success, speedup, task importance and user selection. Its findings reinforce that observed use or raw task coverage does not establish reliable automation, occupational replacement or realised productivity, while offering a more concrete method for estimating selective deployment effects.
qs: Task success helps assess whether tasks can be automated effectively (can a task be automated at all?) and efficiently (how many attempts would it take to automate a task?).
This suggests that even 90% task coverage does not necessarily indicate large job impacts, since Claude may fail on key covered tasks or miss the most time-intensive ones.

kp.k: Evidence measures Claude usage, not economy-wide employment outcomes
kp.d: Published January 15, 2026, the report analyzes random samples of 1M Claude.ai Free, Pro and Max conversations and 1M first-party API transcripts from November 13–20, 2025, before Opus 4.5. Its findings concern cross-domain AI usage and modeled economic implications, rather than measured restructuring of legal employment. API records are individual prompt-response pairs, sometimes mid-session, whereas Claude.ai records can include multi-turn conversations.
qs: Both samples come from November 13, 2025 to November 20, 2025.
For 1P API data, each record is a prompt-response pair from our sample period which in some instances is mid-session for multi-turn interactions.

kp.k: New economic primitives are model-estimated and directionally validated
kp.d: Anthropic introduces five dimensions—task complexity, human and AI skills, use case, autonomy and success—implemented through nine new classifiers. Success is Claude's assessment, not independent verification of completed work. Validation used a small set of permissioned consumer transcripts and internal/synthetic API data; neither validation source fully represents production traffic. Education measures estimate schooling needed to understand text, not users' actual qualifications.
qs: Task success*** measures Claude’s assessment of whether Claude completes tasks successfully.
We selected a final set of nine new classifiers for the five primitives, all of which are directionally accurate even if they may deviate somewhat from human ratings.
none of the measures should be taken as exact or definitive

kp.k: Usage remains concentrated in coding and selected workflows
kp.d: In November 2025, the ten leading tasks represented 24% of Claude.ai usage, versus 23% in August and 21% in January; first-party API concentration increased from 28% to 32% between August and November. Software error correction alone represented 6% of consumer usage and one in ten API records. Chapter 1 reports computer and mathematical tasks at 34% of consumer conversations and 46% of API traffic, with educational usage reaching 15% on Claude.ai.
qs: The most prevalent task in November 2025—modifying software to correct errors—alone represented 6% of usage.
The ten most common tasks grew from 28% of API records in August to 32% in November.
Such usage has risen steadily since our first report, up from 9% of conversations on Claude.ai in January 2025 to 15% in November.

kp.k: Consumer collaboration rebounded while API automation remained dominant
kp.d: Between August and November 2025, Claude.ai augmentation increased 5 percentage points to 52%, while automation declined 4 points to 45%. Directive conversations fell 7 points to 32%, with increased task iteration driving the collaborative shift. API usage remained approximately three-quarters automated and 64% directive. Anthropic suggests product changes may explain some movement and notes that classification changed from Sonnet 4 to Sonnet 4.5, potentially affecting comparisons.
qs: The share of conversations classified as augmented jumped 5pp to 52% and the share deemed automated fell 4pp to 45%.
The rise in augmented use was driven mainly by users iterating with Claude to complete tasks (“task iteration”) rather than asking Claude to explain concepts (“learning”).
In this report we use Sonnet 4.5 for classification whereas in our previous Economic Index report we used Sonnet 4.

kp.k: Automation and decision-making autonomy are distinct
kp.d: The report separates interaction patterns focused on task completion from the amount of discretion delegated to Claude. A narrowly specified task can be automated without requiring substantial autonomous judgment. API usage exhibits greater automation but lower average autonomy than consumer usage; complex consumer tasks receive slightly more autonomy, while API autonomy stays lower across complexity levels.
qs: AI autonomy captures something different from our existing automation/augmentation distinction.
For example, “Translate this paragraph into French” is high automation (directive, minimal back-and-forth) but low AI autonomy (the task requires little decision-making from Claude).
Claude.ai users give the AI slightly more autonomy when working on more complex tasks.

kp.k: Enterprise deployments emphasize work and routine back-office automation
kp.d: Work accounts for 74% of API usage versus 46% of consumer usage; consumer use additionally comprises 19% coursework and 35% personal activity. Chapter 1 reports office and administrative support at 13% of API traffic in November and interprets its growth as evidence of increasing routine workflow automation, including email, document processing, customer relationship management and scheduling. These are provider-reported usage patterns, not measured staffing reductions.
qs: Overall, Claude.ai use is 46% work, 19% coursework, and 35% personal.
Overall, API usage is overwhelmingly work-related (74% vs. 46%) and directive (64% vs. 32%), with three-quarters of interactions classified as automation compared to less than half on Claude.ai
this suggests that businesses are increasingly using Claude to automate routine back-office workflows such as email management, document processing, customer relationship management, and scheduling.

kp.k: Consumer interactions show higher estimated success than API records
kp.d: Claude.ai tasks have estimated unaided human durations of 3.1 hours versus 1.7 hours for API tasks, with AI-assisted durations of 15 versus 5 minutes. Estimated success is 67% versus 49%. Anthropic proposes that clarification and iteration may contribute to the consumer advantage, but platform comparisons are constrained by observing full consumer conversations against isolated API pairs. Personal tasks show 78% estimated success versus 61% for software development.
qs: Claude.ai also shows higher task success rates (67% vs. 49%), which may reflect the benefits of multi-turn conversation, where users can clarify, correct course, and iterate toward a solution.
Claude assesses personal tasks as successfully completed 78% of the time, versus 61% for software development.
This means we can only analyze them as isolated user-assistant pairs rather than full conversation trajectories.

kp.k: Regional adoption converges domestically but remains unequal globally
kp.d: From August to November 2025, the US usage-index Gini declined from 0.37 to 0.32, while international concentration was essentially unchanged. Workforce composition explains nearly two-thirds of cross-state usage-index variation: each 1% increase in the computer/mathematical worker share is associated with 0.36% higher per-capita usage. Models imply US convergence within 2–5 years if recent trends persist, but the report stresses the three-month observation window, sampling noise and imprecise instrumental-variable estimates.
qs: the Gini coefficient, a standard measure of equality, fell from 0.37 to 0.32.
Quantitatively, each 1% increase in the share of such tech workers in a state is associated with 0.36% higher usage per capita
This estimate comes with a high degree of uncertainty as the precision of our estimates cannot rule out much slower rates of diffusion.
we see no evidence that low-use countries are catching up or that high-use countries are pulling away.

kp.k: Income correlates with adoption and different use cases
kp.d: Internationally, a 1% increase in GDP per capita is associated with 0.7% higher Claude usage per capita. Higher-income countries have more work and personal use, whereas lower-income countries emphasize coursework. Higher-usage countries also show more augmentation and less delegated autonomy. The report offers adoption maturity, ability to pay and resource availability as possible explanations, explicitly avoiding causal identification.
qs: At the country level, a 1% increase in GDP per capita is associated with a 0.7% increase in Claude usage per capita.
work use cases and personal use cases of Claude are more common in higher income countries, while coursework use cases are more common in lower income countries
Importantly, the primitives themselves are not necessarily causal factors—we don't know if income or education are truly driving adoption, or if they're proxies for other underlying conditions.

kp.k: Prompt sophistication closely tracks response sophistication
kp.d: Estimated education requirements for prompts and responses correlate at r = 0.925 across 117 countries and r = 0.928 across 50 US-state observations, both p < 0.001. Anthropic interprets this as suggesting that effective use depends on human capital and model design. Relationships between education and success vary by geography: negative internationally, positive across US states before controls, and insignificant within states after controlling for other primitives.
qs: While Claude is able to respond in a highly sophisticated manner, it tends to do so only when users input sophisticated prompts.
task success is negatively associated with human education at the country level, but positively related at the US state level.

kp.k: Complex tasks offer greater speedups but lower reliability
kp.d: At the O*NET task level, Claude-estimated consumer speedups rise from 9x for prompts requiring 12 years of schooling to 12x for those requiring 16 years. Success declines from approximately 70% for below-high-school tasks to 66% for college-level tasks. Discounting for success or excluding low-success tasks does not remove the higher-education productivity gradient. Automation shares, however, are approximately unrelated to education requirements on either platform.
qs: prompts requiring 12 years of schooling (a high school education) enjoy a speedup of 9x, while those requiring 16 years of schooling (a college degree) attain a 12x speedup.
complex tasks still show greater net productivity gains.
On both Claude.ai and 1P API, tasks across education levels show automation patterns in roughly equal shares.

kp.k: Real-world task horizons reflect capability and user selection
kp.d: API estimated success declines from around 60% on sub-hour tasks to roughly 45% on tasks taking humans 5+ hours, with a fitted 50% threshold at 3.5 hours. The analogous consumer threshold is an extrapolated 19 hours, potentially reflecting iterative support. The report contrasts these with METR's software-engineering benchmarks—2 hours for Sonnet 4.5 and about 5 hours for Opus 4.5—and warns that self-selected usage is not a controlled test of autonomous capability.
qs: The fitted line crosses the horizontal 50% success line at 3.5 hours
would hit a 50% success rate at about 19 hours.
If users avoid tasks they expect to fail, for example, observed success rates will overstate true capability on the full distribution of potential tasks.
Controlled benchmarks like METR’s measure the frontier of autonomous capability.

kp.k: Effective coverage weights task presence by importance and success
kp.d: Combining reports, 49% of occupations have observed AI usage for at least one-quarter of their tasks, versus 36% in earlier work. Anthropic's new effective-coverage measure weights success by estimated task duration and O*NET frequency, rather than counting tasks equally. Data entry workers rise because only two of nine tasks are covered but these include their dominant activity; microbiologists fall because specialized hands-on research remains uncovered. Occupational exposure is not equivalent to demonstrated displacement.
qs: Combining across reports, 49% of jobs have seen AI usage for at least a quarter of their tasks.
We define effective AI coverage as the percent of a worker’s day that can be performed successfully by Claude.
This is because although only two of their nine tasks are covered, their largest task—reading and entering data from source documents—has high success rates with Claude.
its implications depend on how often these Claude conversations actually displace or augment work that would otherwise be done by humans.

kp.k: Task-level skill estimates reveal variation within legal support
kp.d: The report trains a task-embedding model against occupation-level BLS education data to estimate task-level schooling requirements. Its legal example illustrates within-occupation heterogeneity: Legal Secretaries is characterized as a 12-year education occupation, but researching laws and court decisions is predicted to require 17.7 years because it resembles lawyers' and paralegals' tasks. This is a modeled skill classification, not a measured legal-AI success rate or demonstrated change in legal staffing.
qs: O*NET doesn't provide task-level education requirements, so we train a model that predicts years of schooling from task embeddings, using the BLS's occupation-level education as the target

For example, Legal Secretaries is a 12-year education occupation, but the task “Review legal publications and perform database searches to identify laws and court decisions relevant to pending cases” is predicted to require 17.7 years because it resembles tasks typically performed by lawyers and paralegals.

kp.k: Hypothetical task removal generally deskills remaining work
kp.d: Predicted schooling averages 13.2 years across economy-wide tasks and 14.4 years among Claude-observed tasks. Removing covered tasks therefore lowers remaining task skill requirements overall. Examples include technical writers, travel agents and some teaching occupations; real estate managers instead retain more negotiation and stakeholder-management work. These are conditional task-removal exercises, not observed employment changes. Wage and employment implications are drawn conditionally from Autor and Thompson's framework, whose expertise concept differs from the report's education proxy.
qs: The mean predicted education for tasks in the economy is 13.2 years.
For tasks that we see in our data, the mean prediction is about a year higher, 14.4 years
Overall, the net first-order impact is to deskill jobs, since AI removes tasks that require relatively higher levels of education.
However, our education-based measure differs from Autor and Thompson's expertise concept

kp.k: Reliability adjustments substantially reduce projected aggregate productivity gains
kp.d: The report reproduces a modeled 1.8-percentage-point annual US labor-productivity growth increase over the next decade under widespread adoption of current capabilities and usage patterns. Multiplying task-level efficiency gains by estimated success reduces this to 1.2 points for Claude.ai and 1.0 for API usage. These are projections, not realized gains or direct measurements of verification time; results also depend on including tasks observed at least 200 times in each 1M-record sample.
qs: If workers must validate AI output, the productivity benefits will be smaller than raw speedups suggest.
implied productivity growth falls from 1.8 to 1.2 percentage points per year for the next decade based on Claude.ai usage, and to 1.0 percentage points for API traffic.
We choose a threshold of 0. 02% because it replicates our previous results

kp.k: Unaccelerated bottleneck tasks constrain productivity and reshape value
kp.d: A constant-elasticity-of-substitution model makes projected gains conditional on how easily tasks substitute for one another. At an elasticity of 0.5, complementary tasks reduce unadjusted annual gains to 0.7–0.9 percentage points; reliability-adjusted estimates are 0.8 for Claude.ai and 0.6 for API. At 1.5, specialization raises unadjusted gains to 2.2–2.6 points. Separately, the report cites Gans and Goldfarb's argument that partial automation can increase labor income by raising bottleneck tasks' value until full job automation.
qs: When the elasticity of substitution is less than one, tasks are complements and those tasks that are not sped up by AI become bottlenecks for broader productivity gains.
Additionally adjusting for task success further reduces the implied productivity effects to 0.8pp
and 0.6pp for API.
partial AI automation can lead to an increase in labor income as such tasks increase in economic value

kp.k: Expertise may complement AI rather than simply be displaced
kp.d: The report qualifies its deskilling exercise: Claude struggles most with complex tasks, potentially preserving the value of professionals who understand and assess its work. It predicts that greater capabilities could expand success and task coverage, while use may shift toward autonomy and production API deployment. Its policy conclusion is that access alone is insufficient: human-capital development, especially in lower-income economies, is necessary for broadly distributed benefits.
qs: Rather than displacing highly skilled professionals, this could instead reinforce the value of their complementary expertise in understanding AI's work and assessing its quality.
tasks that prove automatable may graduate from interactive chat to API deployment.
For AI to benefit users globally, expanding access alone will not suffice—developing the human capital that enables effective use, particularly in lower-income economies, is essential.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Appel, Massenkoff, McCrory and their Anthropic coauthors claim that AI is changing task performance and occupational exposure unevenly: more complex tasks offer greater estimated time savings but lower reliability, while aggregate productivity gains depend on reliability and task complementarity.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain economic report, not a legal-services forecast. Its principal claims concern Claude usage and potential economy-wide effects. Augmentation returned to predominance on Claude.ai, reaching 52% of conversations against 45% automation, whereas roughly three-quarters of first-party API interactions were classified as automation. The authors interpret rising administrative API usage as suggesting increased automation of back-office workflows. Their estimates associate more education-intensive tasks with larger speedups but lower success rates. Combining observations across reports, 49% of occupations have Claude usage covering at least a quarter of their tasks; the authors argue that coverage weighted by time, frequency and success better captures potential occupational exposure. A hypothetical removal of AI-covered tasks produces net deskilling because covered tasks tend to require more education, although the authors also suggest that imperfect performance could reinforce the value of skilled professionals' complementary expertise. Their baseline projection of an additional 1.8 percentage points of annual US labor-productivity growth over a decade falls to 1.2 points using Claude.ai data and 1.0 point using API data after reliability adjustment. Task bottlenecks can reduce gains further. Geographically, the authors find persistent international inequality in usage but early convergence across US states.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of Anthropic's observational Claude-usage samples and model-generated classifications, supplemented by occupational data, external validation and economic modelling; projected productivity and employment effects are not observed outcomes.
pts.d: The report analyzes random samples of one million Claude.ai conversations and one million first-party API records from November 13–20, 2025. Claude estimates task duration with and without AI, educational complexity, autonomy and success from anonymized transcripts. Claude.ai records can contain multi-turn conversations, whereas API records are isolated prompt-response pairs. Reported overall success is 67% for Claude.ai and 49% for API, but these are Claude's assessments, not independently verified task-completion rates. Classifier validation uses a small set of permissioned consumer transcripts, internal and synthetic API data, prior comparisons of estimated versus actual software-engineering time, and correlations with BLS occupational education. Effective coverage combines inferred success and task duration with O*NET task frequency. The deskilling exercise predicts task-level education from task embeddings using Ridge regression and occupation-level BLS education, then removes covered tasks. Productivity projections aggregate estimated task speedups using Hulten's theorem and alternative CES task-substitution assumptions. METR supplies a separate controlled benchmark comparison, not the source of Anthropic's usage-based success estimates. US diffusion estimates use August-to-November comparisons, including instrumental-variable specifications. The report cites outside labor-market research but does not itself establish observed AI-caused changes in employment or wages.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings describe November 2025 usage before Opus 4.5; the longer-term claims are conditional extrapolations rather than unconditional forecasts.
pts.d: Published January 15, 2026, the report mainly compares August and November 2025, with some usage comparisons extending to January 2025. Its productivity projections assume widespread adoption and a one-time productivity gain materializing over the following decade alongside capital deepening. Reliability discounts and alternative degrees of within-job task complementarity materially change the results. Output checking is identified as a reason raw speedups may overstate benefits, but its time cost is not directly measured as a separate verification workload. The estimated US convergence period of 2–5 years extrapolates only three months of change; some specifications describe closing 90% of the log usage gap rather than literal equalization, and the authors explicitly allow much slower diffusion. The roughly 3.5-hour API effective task horizon and extrapolated 19-hour Claude.ai horizon depend on task selection and interaction patterns and are not equivalent to autonomous benchmark horizons. Deskilling requires the assumption that AI-covered tasks actually shrink or disappear from human responsibilities. Wage and employment implications for specific occupations depend on interpreting the report's education proxy through an external expertise framework; the authors acknowledge that the concepts differ. Future capability gains and changes in users' task choices could alter coverage, success and occupational consequences.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The report identifies heterogeneous implications for knowledge workers, administrative workers, firms, consumers and countries; it does not make a distinct forecast for law-firm markets or legal employment.
pts.d: Software and mathematical work dominates observed use, while businesses increasingly deploy Claude in routine administrative workflows such as email management, document processing and scheduling. Data-entry workers have high effective coverage because covered tasks account for much of their working day. Medical transcriptionists and radiologists also rise in the authors' time- and success-weighted exposure measure, whereas microbiologists retain time-intensive physical laboratory work. Technical writers, travel agents and several teaching occupations lose relatively education-intensive tasks in the hypothetical removal exercise; real estate managers retain negotiation, professional judgment and stakeholder-management tasks and therefore show potential upskilling. Under a conditional application of Autor and Thompson's framework, the authors suggest lower wages and higher employment for technical writers and travel agents, and higher wages but lower employment for real estate managers—not measured labor-market outcomes. Skilled professionals may retain value through understanding and assessing AI work. Higher-income countries use Claude more intensively and collaboratively, while lower-income countries have greater coursework shares, raising questions about unequal benefits and complementary human capital. The legal example is methodological: legal secretaries' research into laws and decisions receives a predicted education requirement of 17.7 years despite the occupation's 12-year education classification. This is not a prediction that lawyers, paralegals or legal secretaries will be displaced, nor a finding about legal-AI accuracy.
